passages.title: When a museum changes a label

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A fictional museum at Ashcombe rewrote labels in its geology gallery after visitors said that unfamiliar terminology made the displays difficult to follow. The first draft replaced technical words with everyday descriptions. A curator warned that removing every specialist term would prevent visitors from learning the vocabulary needed to explore the subject further. The final version retained key terms and explained them through examples.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The museum compared two versions of a label beside the same mineral display on alternate days. Staff asked visitors to explain the main process in their own words rather than merely say whether they liked the text. Responses suggested that a short example helped people describe the process. However, the groups were not randomly assigned, and weekend visitors often included more families. Staff treated the result as a reason to refine the labels, not as definitive proof of a universal design rule.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: An audio description was added for visitors who preferred listening. Its script included details that could be felt on a replica, which visitors were permitted to touch. The museum kept a record of label revisions so that later evaluations could identify exactly what had changed. It had not tested whether visitors remembered the explanations several weeks later. The team planned a follow-up study but recognised that people willing to return might differ from other visitors.
